title: You Need a Plan to Get Into Harvard and Stanford MBA
summary: An early, casual episode where the hosts share their weekly roses and thorns, launch a book club segment, and then explain how they 'manifested' getting into Harvard Business School and Stanford GSB using the same life-planning methods they still use: annual vision boards, a backwards-planned 'adult planned-out life' spreadsheet, a 70-item yearly aspiration list scored out of 35, and writing everything down. Main takeaway: set a goal (even a changeable one), visualize it daily, and work backwards to a timeline of concrete steps.

ideas.idea: Create a vision board every year around January by cutting out magazine images and words on gut instinct, then revisit, reinvent and reinvest in it multiple times a year.
ideas.detail: Jean taught Cherie the practice; Cherie's 2015 board was word-heavy and career-focused because she was anxious about getting a job, while Jean's are mostly photos of things she loves. Doing it with friends reveals how differently people approach it.

ideas.idea: Put your vision board somewhere you see it every day; the daily visual reminder of what you want your life to look like is where the power comes from.
ideas.detail: Jean describes making a vision board as vulnerable because it is a visualization of all your hopes and dreams; she also made a second board mid-year for the first time.

ideas.idea: Plan business school by working backwards from the goal in a spreadsheet with columns for age, milestone and deadline.
ideas.detail: Cherie's 'Adult Planned-Out Life' Google Sheet: graduate in 2024 means enroll in 2022 at 26-27, submit applications more than a year before that, and take the GRE/GMAT, study and secure recommendation letters even earlier.

ideas.idea: The first step is having a goal, but goals need not be fixed; they change on macro and micro levels and sometimes life changes them for you.
ideas.detail: At 21 as a Goldman Sachs analyst Jean's goal was to become a Goldman partner; two years later she wanted out entirely. Without a goal you have nothing to work toward.

ideas.idea: Have a plan, but plans are written in pencil.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned this from 77-year-old professor Joel Peterson's Stanford class 'Engineering a Remarkable Life', whose final assignment was a 10-page life plan covering career, spouse and children.

ideas.idea: Write a yearly list of about 70 aspirations across life categories and score yourself out of 35, so hitting half counts as 100%.
ideas.detail: Jean's list mixes easy lifts, recurring habits like gym three times a week, stretch goals and a separate longer-term bucket list; categories include health and wellness, family, friendships and relationships. Cherie has copied the practice.

ideas.idea: Aspirations should be tangible and intentional, like 'dinner with Sarah five times' or 'try this specific bakery', not just lofty goals.
ideas.detail: Writing down that you want quality time with a close friend is the only way you'll remember to schedule it; small items like a bakery visit or a monthly hike with 12 check boxes give easy wins and track what already brings joy, such as Jean's HBS book club.

ideas.idea: Pre-fill a month-by-month calendar of events you're looking forward to, so dreary stretches like winter have something ahead.
ideas.detail: Jean writes out all 12 months, adds major events as they approach, and keeps it as a running account of her year.

ideas.idea: Get things out of your head and onto paper or a document; unwritten ideas swirl, stress you and disappear.
ideas.detail: Cherie's parting advice: writing everything down is how she stays efficient and how she manifests and visualizes; printing lists and putting them in your closet or bathroom keeps them in your face.

ideas.idea: Give yourself grace to cancel commitments while recovering, rather than showing up as a diminished version of yourself.
ideas.detail: Post-COVID, Jean over-scheduled herself, judged Boston University media venture theses while exhausted and left early; her friend convinced her to skip a Dartmouth Club of LA event. Cherie adds: if you feel guilty canceling, don't commit in the first place.

ideas.idea: A deep-seated fear of being a burden can make you doubt whether even close friends want to celebrate you; name it and let friends reassure you.
ideas.detail: Cherie spiraled when two friends couldn't attend her birthday in San Francisco; her friend Maddie told her 'you're not in the way, you are the way,' and the birthday dinner made her feel loved.

ideas.idea: A friendly book race with a friend or sibling is effective motivation to read again after a dry spell.
ideas.detail: The hosts log every book and compete on annual count; Jean has done this for years and runs an HBS girlfriends' book club. Recent reads: Kevin Kwan's 'Lies and Weddings' (A-minus) and Maye Musk's 'A Woman Makes a Plan' (strong B).

ideas.idea: Secondhand retail is a serious business: Goodwill generates billions in revenue, not junk.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned this preparing a Stanford case when the founder of ThredUp visited class; the hosts also praise the Salvation Army's twice-yearly $2.99 clothing sale.
